title: Catering Basics & Food Safety
subtitle: Plan, cost and deliver party food for 50 to 100 guests that is safe, on time and profitable.
description: A practical course for good home cooks who want to cater birthdays, naming ceremonies, church and office events in Nigeria. You learn the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food and temperature control, how to plan and scale menus with real calculations, how to cost each plate and quote with deposits, and how to hold, transport and serve food safely.
outcomes: Apply the WHO Five Keys and the 5°C to 60°C danger zone rules to every dish you cater
Calculate portions and scale recipes for 50 or 100 guests with a sensible buffer
Cost a job, work out cost per plate and set a price with a chosen profit margin
Plan a production day backwards from serving time, with safe holding and transport
Manage allergens and special diets honestly and prepare labelled allergen-free meals
Write quotations with deposit terms and keep records that improve each job
audience: Women who already cook well for family and community events and want to cater safely and profitably for paying clients.
tools: A smartphone with WhatsApp and a calculator or spreadsheet app (Google Sheets or Excel)
Separate chopping boards for raw and ready-to-eat food
A notebook for job sheets, costings and temperature logs
Your usual pots, gas cooker and serving equipment

modules.title: Safe Catering Foundations
modules.overview: Catering is cooking for people who trust you with their health. This module shows how a catering job runs from first enquiry to final clean-up, teaches the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food in a busy party kitchen, and explains the temperature rules that keep rice, stew and chicken safe for hours.

lessons.title: From home cook to caterer: how a catering job really runs
objectives: Describe the eight stages of a catering job from enquiry to clean-up
Explain three ways catering differs from cooking for your family
Choose a realistic first job size for your kitchen and helpers
Name the common Nigerian event formats and what each demands

blocks.text: If people already ask you to cook for birthdays, naming ceremonies or church events, you have the most important ingredient: food people enjoy. Catering adds three things on top of good cooking. **Scale**: you cook five or ten times more than usual, in bigger pots, with more gas and more hands. **Responsibility**: the people eating are not your family, and some may be elderly, pregnant, very young or allergic. **Time pressure**: the food must be ready, hot and safe at an exact time, in a place that is not your kitchen.

blocks.name: chef
blocks.alt: A cook in a chef's hat preparing food
blocks.caption: Catering starts with good cooking, then adds planning, safety and delivery on top.

blocks.text: The eight stages of every job
Big or small, almost every catering job follows the same path. When you know the path, you stop forgetting things like packaging, serving spoons or the balance payment.

blocks.title: The catering job path
items: Enquiry and details
Quote and deposit
Plan and shop
Prep and cook
Hold, pack, transport
Serve, clean, get paid
blocks.caption: Each stage feeds the next: a vague enquiry leads to a wrong quote, and a wrong quote leads to a loss.

items: **Enquiry**: collect the date, venue, serving time, number of guests, budget, menu wishes and any allergies or special diets.
**Quote**: send a written price per head or per package, with what is included and what is not.
**Deposit**: agree a deposit before you buy anything, so you never fund a client's party from your own pocket.
**Plan and shop**: calculate quantities, write a shopping list and a cooking timetable.
**Prep and cook**: wash, cut, marinate, cook, following food safety rules from the first onion to the last plate.
**Hold, pack and transport**: keep hot food hot and cold food cold until serving.
**Serve**: buffet, plated, or packed food packs handed out by ushers.
**Clean up and get paid**: collect your equipment, receive the balance, and write notes for next time.

blocks.text: Common event formats in Nigeria

head: Format
What it looks like
What it demands from you
rows: Plastic or foil packs of jollof or fried rice, chicken, salad and moi moi, shared by ushers
Many identical portions, fast packing, enough packs and spoons
Guests serve themselves from chafing dishes or coolers
Holding food hot for hours, servers to control portions
Puff puff, spring rolls, samosa, peppered gizzard, mini meat pies
Lots of frying, timing so items stay crisp, small packs or trays
20 to 60 packs delivered by a fixed time
Punctuality, clean labelled packs, receipts for the company

blocks.text: Owambe parties, weddings and burial receptions often combine formats, for example food packs for most guests, a served table for the celebrant's family, and small chops at the start. Each format changes your quantities, your packaging and how many helpers you need.
Choosing your first job size

Your capacity is set by your biggest pot, your number of burners, your fridge or freezer space, your helpers and your transport. A good rule is to start with a job you could almost do twice over, so a delay or a burnt pot does not ruin the event. Many new caterers start with 20 to 50 guests and grow from there.

blocks.title: Worked example: is a 40-pack office lunch realistic?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Ibadan is asked to deliver 40 packs of jollof rice, chicken and coleslaw to an office by 1:00 pm on a weekday. She has a two-burner gas cooker, one large pot, a medium pot and one helper.
steps: She lists the work: about 5 kg of raw rice, 40 chicken pieces, one batch of coleslaw, 40 packs to fill and label.
Her large pot cooks about 3 kg of rice at once, so the rice needs two batches of roughly 75 minutes each, about 2.5 hours.
Chicken boiling and frying on the second burner takes about 2 hours, running at the same time as the rice.
Coleslaw and packing with her helper takes about 1 hour, plus 45 minutes to drive to the office.
Working back from 1:00 pm with a 30-minute buffer, she needs to start cooking by about 7:00 am.
blocks.result: The job fits her equipment if she starts at 7:00 am and preps vegetables the evening before. A 150-pack order the same day would not fit, so she would decline it or hire extra pots and help.

blocks.title: Write everything down
blocks.text: Keep one notebook or one WhatsApp note per job with the client's details, menu, quantities, costs and timings. After three or four jobs this becomes your own planning guide, built from real numbers.

In the rest of this course you will learn the food safety rules that protect your guests, how to plan and scale a menu, how to cost each plate so you make a profit, and how to quote, take deposits and deliver professionally. The capstone asks you to plan a full event for a real or realistic client.

takeaways: Catering adds scale, responsibility and time pressure to good cooking
Every job follows the same path, from enquiry to final payment
Your equipment, helpers and transport set your safe capacity
Start with jobs you could almost do twice over

activity.title: Map your kitchen capacity
steps: List your burners, pots (with rough sizes), fridge or freezer space, coolers and serving dishes.
Note how many reliable helpers you can call and your transport options.
Time yourself cooking your normal biggest pot of rice from start to finish.
Using that time, estimate the largest food-pack order you could deliver by 1:00 pm.
Write the number down as your current safe capacity.
activity.evidence: A one-page capacity note with your equipment list, cooking time and maximum guest number

lessons.title: The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food in a party kitchen
objectives: List the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food in order
Apply each key to a real party menu
Set up handwashing and cleaning routines for a catering day
Prevent cross-contamination between raw and cooked foods

blocks.text: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that almost 1 in 9 people in the world fall ill every year after eating contaminated food. Most of that illness is preventable. WHO teaches food handlers everywhere a simple set of rules called the **Five Keys to Safer Food**. They are easy to remember and they work in a home kitchen, a canteen or a hired kitchen behind an event hall.

blocks.title: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
items: Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
blocks.caption: Check all five keys for every dish on your menu, not only the meat.

blocks.name: wash-hands
blocks.alt: A person washing hands at a sink
blocks.caption: Key 1 starts with hands: wash before cooking and after anything dirty.

blocks.text: Key 1: Keep clean

Germs that cause food poisoning live on hands, cloths, chopping boards and surfaces. Wash your hands with soap and clean running water before handling food, often during cooking, and always after using the toilet, touching raw meat, fish or eggs, handling money, blowing your nose or taking out the rubbish. Rub every part of the hands, including between fingers and under nails, then rinse and dry with a clean towel. If you have no tap, set up a bucket with a tap or ask a helper to pour water.

items: Tie hair back or cover it, remove rings and bracelets, and keep nails short.
Wear a clean apron, and keep it for cooking only.
Wash and sanitise boards, knives and worktops after raw meat or fish.
Keep insects, rats, cats and dogs away from food and the cooking area.
Anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting or an infected cut on the hand should not handle food that day.

blocks.text: Key 2: Separate raw and cooked

**Cross-contamination** means germs moving from raw food to ready-to-eat food. It happens when the same board is used for raw chicken and then for coleslaw cabbage, when raw meat drips onto salad in a fridge, or when the bowl used to marinate chicken is reused for cooked chicken. Use separate boards and knives for raw meat and fish, or wash them well in between. Store raw meat in covered containers below cooked food in the fridge or freezer.
Key 3: Cook thoroughly

Cook meat, poultry, eggs and seafood until the centre reaches **70°C**, the temperature on WHO's Five Keys poster. Chicken juices should run clear, not pink, but a probe thermometer is far more reliable than looking. Bring soups and stews to the boil. When you reheat cooked food, heat it until it is steaming hot all through.
Key 4: Keep food at safe temperatures

Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Keep hot food piping hot, above 60°C, until serving, and keep cold food cold, below 5°C. The next lesson covers this key in detail because it is where most catering problems happen.
Key 5: Use safe water and raw materials

Use safe, treated water for cooking, washing salad and making ice. Buy fresh meat and fish from sellers who keep them cool and clean. Reject swollen, rusted or dented cans, mouldy grains and spices, and food past its expiry date. Wash fruit and vegetables well, especially anything eaten raw like cabbage, carrots, cucumber and lettuce.

blocks.title: Worked example: applying the Five Keys to one menu
blocks.context: For example, Funmi is catering a 60-guest naming ceremony with jollof rice, fried chicken, coleslaw and moi moi.
steps: Keep clean: she sets up a handwashing point with soap and a towel at the kitchen door and asks both helpers to wash on arrival and after every raw-meat task.
Separate: she uses a red board for raw chicken and a green board only for cabbage and carrots, and keeps the coleslaw covered on a separate table.
Cook thoroughly: she checks the thickest chicken pieces with a probe thermometer and confirms 70°C or more before frying.
Safe temperatures: coleslaw stays in a cooler with ice packs, the rice and chicken go hot into insulated coolers.
Safe water and raw materials: she washes the cabbage in treated water and buys eggs for the moi moi from a trusted seller, checking for cracks.
blocks.result: Every dish, not just the chicken, has a clear safety control, and each helper knows their role.

blocks.text: Train your helpers on the Five Keys before every job, not only the first time. A two-minute briefing at the start of the day works well: where the handwashing point is, which board is for raw meat, which table is for ready-to-eat food, and who checks temperatures. Helpers copy what they see, so let them see you wash your hands and change boards every time.

blocks.title: Salads and raw vegetables are high risk
blocks.text: Coleslaw and salad are not cooked, so nothing kills germs that land on them. Wash vegetables in safe water, use clean boards, keep them cold, and dress them as close to serving as you can.

takeaways: The Five Keys: keep clean, separate, cook thoroughly, safe temperatures, safe water and raw materials
Handwashing with soap at the right moments prevents a large share of problems
Use separate boards and storage for raw and ready-to-eat foods
Cook meat to 70°C at the centre and check with a thermometer

activity.title: Five Keys audit of your kitchen
steps: Write the Five Keys down the left side of a page.
Walk through your kitchen and note one thing you already do well for each key.
Note one gap for each key, for example no separate board for raw meat.
Choose the two cheapest fixes and do them this week.
Take a photo of your handwashing point and your separate boards.
activity.evidence: Your Five Keys audit page and before and after photos of two fixes

lessons.title: Temperature control: the danger zone, cooling and reheating
objectives: State the danger zone and the 2-hour rule used by WHO
Hold hot food above 60°C and cold food below 5°C during an event
Cool and store cooked rice, stew and meat safely
Use a probe thermometer correctly and record readings

blocks.text: Bacteria that cause food poisoning grow fastest at warm temperatures, roughly the heat of a Nigerian afternoon. WHO's Five Keys poster marks the range between **5°C and 60°C** as the **danger zone**. Below 5°C growth slows right down. Above 60°C most of these bacteria cannot grow. Between the two, numbers can double quickly. Catering is mostly about keeping food out of this zone, or moving it through quickly.

blocks.name: thermometer
blocks.caption: A cheap probe thermometer tells you the truth about your food's temperature.

blocks.title: Safe temperature path for party food
items: Cook to 70°C centre
Hold above 60°C
Serve within plan
Cool leftovers fast
Store below 5°C
blocks.caption: Food should only pass through the danger zone briefly, on the way up when cooking or on the way down when cooling.

blocks.text: The numbers to remember

head: Rule
Temperature or time
What it means at an event
rows: Check the thickest chicken or turkey piece
Rice, stew and meat stay steaming hot until served
Coleslaw, salad, fruit, cream desserts stay chilled
Cooked food left out longer should not be served
Reheat once only, and only food that was cooled and stored safely

blocks.text: Different countries draw the danger zone slightly differently. For example, the United States Department of Agriculture uses about 4°C to 60°C, and the UK uses 8°C to 63°C for its legal limits. In this course we use WHO's 5°C and 60°C, which is simple and safe.
Why rice needs special care

Cooked rice is one of the riskiest foods at Nigerian parties because so much of it is cooked early and kept warm for hours. Uncooked rice can carry spores of a bacterium called *Bacillus cereus*. Cooking does not kill all the spores. If cooked rice sits warm for hours, the spores grow and make toxins that reheating does not destroy. The answer is simple: keep cooked rice hot above 60°C, or cool it quickly and refrigerate it, never leave it sitting warm on the counter.
Cooling food quickly

items: Spread hot food into shallow trays or several small containers, not one deep pot.
Stand containers in a basin of cold water with ice, stirring stews now and then.
Once steam stops rising, cover and refrigerate, aiming to be below 5°C well within the 2-hour room-temperature limit.
Label each container with the dish and the date it was cooked.
Use refrigerated cooked food within a short time, and when in doubt, throw it out.

blocks.text: Using a probe thermometer

A digital probe thermometer costs far less than one lost client. Push the tip into the thickest part of the meat, away from bone, or into the centre of a pot of rice or stew after stirring. Wait until the number stops changing. Clean the probe with hot soapy water or a sanitiser wipe between foods, especially between raw and cooked. Check it now and then in boiling water: it should read close to 100°C.

blocks.title: Worked example: a holding plan for a 1:00 pm serving
blocks.context: For example, Chioma finishes cooking jollof rice and chicken at 10:30 am for a birthday party that serves food at 1:00 pm. She has two insulated coolers and a probe thermometer.
steps: 10:30 am: she checks the rice at 85°C and the chicken at 78°C, then fills the coolers hot and closes them immediately.
She warms each cooler first with hot water for 10 minutes and empties it, so the cold walls do not chill the food.
12:15 pm at the venue: she opens one cooler briefly and the rice reads 68°C, still above 60°C.
1:00 pm: serving starts, and she keeps lids closed between servings.
3:30 pm: leftover rice reads 52°C, below 60°C, and has been out of safe holding for an unknown time, so she does not take it home for resale.
blocks.result: Her food stayed above 60°C for the whole 2.5-hour hold. She records the readings as evidence of safe practice.

blocks.title: Smell and taste are not safety tests
blocks.text: Food carrying harmful bacteria or toxins can look, smell and taste normal. Do not decide safety by tasting. Decide by time and temperature.

Ice also matters. Ice made from unsafe water can carry germs into drinks and salads, so make ice from treated or boiled and cooled water, or buy it from a seller you trust. Keep ice for drinks separate from ice used to chill coolers and bottles, and never use your hands to scoop it: use a clean scoop or cup.
Write temperatures on a simple log sheet: dish, time, reading, initials. It takes seconds, it trains your helpers, and it gives you evidence if a client ever asks how you keep food safe.

takeaways: The danger zone in this course is 5°C to 60°C
Hold hot food above 60°C and cold food below 5°C
Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours
Cool food fast in shallow containers, and take special care with rice
Use a probe thermometer and write the readings down

activity.title: Run a temperature test
steps: Cook a normal pot of rice or stew and measure the centre temperature when it is done.
Pack it into your cooler or food flask and measure again after 1, 2 and 3 hours.
Record each reading on a log sheet with the time.
Note when, if ever, it fell below 60°C.
Decide how long you can safely hold food with your current equipment.
activity.evidence: A completed temperature log showing your cooler's real holding time

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food?
options: Add extra salt to preserve stew
Taste food to check if it is safe
Cover food with a cloth outdoors
quiz.explain: The Five Keys are keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials.

quiz.q: Funmi used a board for raw chicken and now wants to cut cabbage for coleslaw. What should she do?
options: Wipe the board with a dry cloth
Rinse it quickly in a basin of water
Use a separate clean board, or wash and sanitise this one first
Cut the cabbage on the same board, since it will be dressed
quiz.explain: Coleslaw is not cooked, so germs from raw chicken would reach guests. A separate or properly cleaned board prevents cross-contamination.

quiz.q: In this course, what is the danger zone?
options: Any food left in the sun
quiz.explain: WHO's Five Keys poster marks 5°C to 60°C as the danger zone, where bacteria grow quickly.

quiz.q: Rice finished cooking at 9:00 am and sat on the counter, warm, until 1:30 pm. What is the safest decision?
options: Reheat it until very hot and serve it
Serve it, because it smells fine
Do not serve it, because it sat warm for over 2 hours
Add fresh stew to it and serve
quiz.explain: Cooked rice left warm for hours can grow Bacillus cereus toxins that reheating does not destroy. More than 2 hours at room temperature means do not serve.

quiz.q: What is the best way to check that fried chicken pieces were cooked thoroughly before frying?
options: Check that the outside is golden brown
Use a probe thermometer in the thickest piece and confirm 70°C or more
Cook for the same time as last week
Press the meat with a spoon
quiz.explain: Colour can mislead. A probe thermometer in the thickest part confirms the 70°C centre temperature from the Five Keys.

quiz.q: Amaka can cook about 50 packs comfortably by 1:00 pm. A client asks for 150 packs on the same day. What is the most professional response?
options: Accept and hope to cook faster
Accept and leave out the food safety checks to save time
Decline, or offer it only if she hires extra pots and trained help
quiz.explain: Taking a job far beyond capacity leads to shortcuts and lateness. Declining or adding real capacity protects guests and her reputation.

modules.title: Menus, Portions and Production Day
modules.overview: Here you turn a client's wishes into a workable menu, calculate exactly how much to buy for 50 or 100 guests, and run the cooking day with a timetable that works backwards from serving time. You also learn how to hold and transport food so it arrives safe, hot and neat.

lessons.title: Planning an event menu that holds well and pleases guests
objectives: Collect the event details that shape a menu
Choose dishes that hold safely for the time between cooking and serving
Balance a menu across starch, protein, vegetables and extras
Match the menu to your kitchen capacity and the client's budget

blocks.text: A good event menu is not just a list of dishes you cook well. It is a set of dishes that suit the guests, survive the journey, stay safe for hours, fit your equipment and fit the client's budget. Before you suggest anything, ask the right questions.
Questions to ask before you plan

items: Date, venue and the exact serving time. Is there a kitchen or power at the venue?
Number of adult guests and children, and whether guests come and go or sit at once.
Format: food packs, buffet, served table or small chops.
Budget per head or total budget.
Must-have dishes, for example jollof rice, fried rice, ofada with ayamase, pounded yam and egusi, or asun.
Allergies, religious needs such as no pork, and vegetarian guests.
Who serves: your staff, the client's ushers, or guests themselves.

blocks.name: curry-and-rice
blocks.alt: A plate of rice with stew
blocks.caption: Rice dishes travel and hold well, which is why they anchor most Nigerian party menus.

blocks.text: Build the plate first

Think of one guest's plate. A balanced Nigerian party plate usually has a **starch** (jollof or fried rice, ofada, swallow), a **protein** (chicken, beef, turkey, fish), a **side** (moi moi, plantain, coleslaw or salad) and sometimes a **small extra** (a bottle of water, a small chops pack). Planning by plate helps you count portions and price per head later.
Pick dishes that hold well

Some foods stay good in a hot cooler for three hours. Others go soggy, dry or unsafe. Fried plantain softens, salad wilts once dressed, and pounded yam forms a skin and hardens. Jollof rice, fried rice, stews, moi moi and well-cooked meats hold better. Plan the hard-to-hold items for last-minute work, or swap them out.

blocks.title: Choosing dishes by holding and prep time
items: Easy wins: jollof, stew
Worth it: moi moi, asun
Last-minute: dodo, salad dressing
Avoid for big jobs: fresh swallow
blocks.caption: Fill most of the menu from the top row and schedule bottom-row items as late as possible.

blocks.title: Worked example: from budget to menu
blocks.context: For example, Halima is asked to cater an 80-guest wedding introduction in Kaduna. The client's budget is about ₦4,500 per head (approximate) and food is served as packs at 2:00 pm, 50 minutes from her kitchen.
steps: She builds one plate: jollof rice, one piece of chicken, moi moi, coleslaw, and a bottle of water.
She drops fried plantain because it would be soft after a 3-hour hold, and offers it only if the client pays for an extra hand to fry at the venue.
She checks capacity: two big pots of rice, one pot for moi moi in leaves or tins, chicken boiled and fried on the third burner.
She asks about allergies and learns one guest cannot eat groundnut, so no groundnut-based pepper mix goes on the chicken.
She sends the client two options: Option A as above, and Option B with fried rice and turkey at a higher price.
blocks.result: The client gets a clear, costed choice, and every dish on it can be cooked, held and delivered safely with Halima's equipment.

blocks.text: Match the menu to your capacity

Count the pots and burners each dish needs and how long it takes. If three dishes all need the big pot at 8:00 am, the plan fails. Dishes that can be made the day before and chilled safely, like moi moi steamed and cooled quickly, or stew base, spread the load. Anything prepared ahead must be cooled fast, refrigerated below 5°C and reheated until steaming hot.

head: Dish
Make ahead?
Holding notes
rows: Cool quickly, chill, reheat by steaming until hot through
Boil early, fry on the day
Hold hot, do not stack wet pieces

blocks.title: Offer packages, not endless choice
blocks.text: Give clients two or three fixed packages with clear prices. It makes quoting faster, shopping simpler and portions easier to control than building a fresh menu for every enquiry.
Packs versus buffet: how format changes the menu

With food packs you control every portion, because you fill each pack yourself before leaving your kitchen. With a buffet, guests serve themselves and early guests often take more, so later guests can find empty dishes. For a buffet, put trained servers behind the main dishes, use a set serving spoon for rice and tongs for one piece of meat, and plan a slightly bigger buffer. Children's packs can be smaller, which you should agree and price separately with the client.

Write the final menu with portion sizes beside each item, for example one piece of chicken, one wrap of moi moi, two serving spoons of rice. This one page becomes the base for your quantities, costing and packing list in the next lessons.

takeaways: Ask about serving time, format, budget, guests and allergies before planning
Plan one balanced plate, then multiply
Choose dishes that hold well, and schedule fragile ones last
Check that the menu fits your pots, burners and time

activity.title: Write two menu packages
steps: Choose a realistic event, for example a 50-guest birthday with food packs.
Write Package A and Package B, each with starch, protein, side and an extra.
Mark each dish as make-ahead, cook on the day or last-minute.
Note the holding method for each dish.
Remove or replace any dish that cannot hold safely for 3 hours.
activity.evidence: A one-page menu sheet with two packages, portion sizes and holding notes

lessons.title: Portioning and scaling recipes for 50 and 100 guests
objectives: Set a portion size for each dish and test it
Calculate total quantities for 50 and 100 guests with a safety buffer
Scale a recipe using a scaling factor
Convert quantities into a shopping list in market units

blocks.text: Running out of food at a party is embarrassing. Cooking far too much wastes money and leaves you with leftovers you should not sell. The fix is simple arithmetic done honestly: **portion size × number of guests + a buffer = total quantity**.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person using a large calculator
blocks.caption: Quantities come from simple multiplication, not guesswork.

blocks.title: From guest count to shopping list
items: Portion per guest
Multiply by guests
Add 10% buffer
Convert to raw weight
Round to market units
blocks.caption: Do the same five steps for every dish on the menu.

blocks.text: Step 1: Set and test your portion sizes

Portion sizes are your decision, so test them. Cook a measured amount of raw rice, then serve it with your usual serving spoon into your usual pack and count how many packs it fills. That tells you your real raw rice per guest. Many caterers find somewhere around 100 g to 150 g of raw rice per adult for a full plate, but your spoon, your pack and your guests decide your number. Write it down.

head: Item
Example portion per adult
How to check
rows: Cook 1.2 kg and count how many packs it fills
Decide how many pieces you cut each bird into
Count wraps from one measured batch of beans
Weigh one serving spoon of finished coleslaw

blocks.text: Step 2 and 3: Multiply and add a buffer

Multiply each portion by the number of guests. Then add a buffer, usually around 10 percent, because guest numbers grow, servers give bigger spoons and some food is lost when packing. Children may eat less, so if the client says 100 guests including 30 children, you may plan the children at a smaller pack size. Agree the final number in writing.

blocks.title: Worked example: jollof rice and chicken for 50 and 100 guests
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi uses her tested portions: 120 g raw rice and one chicken piece per adult. She cuts each bird into 8 pieces. She plans a 10% buffer.
steps: Rice for 50 guests: 50 × 120 g = 6,000 g = 6 kg. Add 10%: 6 × 1.1 = 6.6 kg. She buys 7 kg.
Rice for 100 guests: 100 × 120 g = 12 kg. Add 10%: 12 × 1.1 = 13.2 kg. She buys 14 kg.
Chicken for 50 guests: 50 pieces × 1.1 = 55 pieces. 55 ÷ 8 = 6.9, so she buys 7 birds.
Chicken for 100 guests: 100 × 1.1 = 110 pieces. 110 ÷ 8 = 13.75, so she buys 14 birds.
Coleslaw for 100 guests: 100 × 80 g = 8 kg, plus 10% = 8.8 kg of finished coleslaw.
blocks.result: For 100 guests she shops for 14 kg of rice, 14 birds and enough cabbage, carrots and dressing to make about 9 kg of coleslaw, with a small buffer and no wild over-buying.

blocks.text: Scaling a recipe

Your home recipe may serve 10. To scale it, find the **scaling factor**: new number of servings ÷ original number of servings. For 100 guests from a recipe for 10, the factor is 100 ÷ 10 = 10. Multiply every ingredient by 10. For 50 guests, the factor is 5.

blocks.title: Worked example: scaling a jollof base from 10 to 50 servings
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's family jollof for 10 uses 1.2 kg rice, 1 kg tomato and pepper blend, 300 g onions, 250 ml vegetable oil and 1.2 litres of stock.
steps: Scaling factor: 50 ÷ 10 = 5.
Rice: 1.2 kg × 5 = 6 kg. Blend: 1 kg × 5 = 5 kg. Onions: 300 g × 5 = 1.5 kg.
Oil: 250 ml × 5 = 1.25 litres. Stock: 1.2 litres × 5 = 6 litres.
Salt, stock cubes and pepper: she starts with about three-quarters of the scaled amount, then tastes and adjusts.
Her biggest pot holds about 3 kg of rice, so she cooks two batches of 3 kg, each with half the scaled ingredients.
blocks.result: She has a clear scaled recipe and knows it must be cooked in two batches, which she adds to her cooking timetable.

blocks.title: Not everything scales in a straight line
blocks.text: Seasoning, liquid and cooking time do not always multiply perfectly. Big pots lose less water to steam, and strong spices add up fast. Season gradually and taste. Never cram a pot beyond its size: rice cooks unevenly and the bottom burns.
Step 5: Round to market units

Markets sell in bags, crates, baskets and local measures that vary from place to place. Turn your totals into what you will actually buy: kilograms of rice, a crate of eggs (30 eggs), a number of whole birds, litres of oil. If you buy by a local measure, weigh one measure at home once so your list matches reality. Keep the list in the same order as the market route to save time.

takeaways: Portion × guests + about 10% buffer = total quantity
Test portions with your own spoon and pack
Scaling factor = new servings ÷ original servings
Season gradually when scaling, and cook in batches that fit your pots
Round totals to the units you actually buy

activity.title: Build a 100-guest quantity sheet
steps: Test your rice portion by cooking 1 kg of raw rice and counting packs.
Write portion sizes for every dish on one of your menu packages.
Calculate totals for 50 and 100 guests with a 10% buffer.
Scale one of your recipes using the scaling factor.
Turn the totals into a shopping list in market units.
activity.evidence: A quantity sheet showing every calculation for 50 and 100 guests

lessons.title: Production day: timetable, cross-contamination control and safe transport
objectives: Build a cooking timetable working backwards from serving time
Organise the kitchen into raw and ready-to-eat zones
Pack, load and transport hot and cold food safely
Prepare an equipment checklist so nothing is forgotten

blocks.text: Production day is where planning meets the pot. A clear timetable, a tidy kitchen layout and a packed equipment box let you stay calm, keep food safe and arrive on time. Most catering disasters come from no buffer time, not from bad cooking.
Work backwards from serving time

Start from the moment guests eat and walk backwards: set-up time at the venue, travel time, loading, packing, and each cooking task. Add a buffer for traffic, a late gas refill or a power cut. The aim is to finish cooking close enough to serving that food can be held hot safely, but not so late that you rush.

blocks.title: Working back from a 1:00 pm serving
items: 6:30 am start cooking
10:00 am cooking done
10:15 am pack hot
11:00 am depart
11:45 am set up
1:00 pm serve
blocks.caption: The 15 to 45 minute gaps are deliberate buffers, not wasted time.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 100-pack timetable
blocks.context: For example, Ronke caters 100 packs of jollof rice, chicken, moi moi and coleslaw for a 1:00 pm church anniversary, 45 minutes away. She has a three-burner cooker, two helpers and preheated coolers.
steps: Day before: shop, steam moi moi and cool it fast in shallow trays, make stew base and refrigerate, wash and shred cabbage and carrots, chill.
6:30 am: boil chicken on burner 1, start rice batch 1 on burner 2, heat stew base to boiling on burner 3.
8:30 am: rice batch 2; fry chicken in turns; reheat moi moi by steaming until hot through.
10:00 am: probe-check chicken at 70°C or above and rice above 60°C; mix coleslaw dressing and keep it cold.
10:15 to 10:45 am: pack food into preheated coolers, coleslaw into an ice-packed cooler; 11:00 am leave; 11:45 am arrive and set up.
blocks.result: Food is cooked by 10:00 am, held hot for 3 hours or less, and Ronke has 75 minutes of buffer between arrival and serving.

blocks.name: delivery-truck
blocks.alt: A delivery van on the road
blocks.caption: Transport is part of food safety: food must travel hot, cold and covered.

blocks.text: Zones that stop cross-contamination

items: **Raw zone**: one table and board for raw chicken, meat and fish, with its own knife and a bin.
**Cooking zone**: burners and pots, with clean spoons that never touch raw meat.
**Ready-to-eat zone**: coleslaw, packing and serving, wiped and sanitised, away from raw work.
Wash hands every time you move from the raw zone to any other zone.
Use colour-coded or clearly marked boards and bowls, and keep cooked food covered.

blocks.text: Holding and transport

Preheat insulated coolers with hot water for 10 minutes, empty them and fill with very hot food. Fill them well, because a half-empty cooler loses heat faster. Keep cold foods in a separate cooler with ice packs. Load coolers flat, wedge them so they cannot slide, and never put raw items in the same box as ready food. At the venue, keep lids closed until serving and check temperatures.
Equipment checklist

head: Group
Items
rows: Pots, gas cylinder with spare, burners, ladles, frying spider, probe thermometer
Insulated coolers, ice packs, chafing dishes with fuel, foil, lids
Food packs, spoons, serviettes, serving spoons, tongs, labels, nylon bags
Soap, hand towels, sanitiser, clean cloths, gloves, aprons, hair covers, bin bags
Menu, guest count, temperature log, client phone number, receipt book

blocks.title: Gas cylinder safety
blocks.text: Keep LPG cylinders upright, outside or in a well-ventilated space, away from the flame. Check hoses and joints with soapy water: bubbles mean a leak. If you smell gas, turn off the cylinder, do not switch lights or phones on or off nearby, and open doors and windows.
Serving safely at the venue

The last hour is where good work is often undone. Guests crowd the table, helpers are tired and dishes are left open in the heat. Set up a serving station before guests arrive: a clean table, chafing dishes lit and hot, serving spoons and tongs for each dish, and a covered spare cooler under the table. Keep a bowl of soapy water or a bottle of sanitiser and clean cloths nearby for spills.

items: Servers wash hands before serving and use tongs or spoons, never bare hands, for ready-to-eat food.
Refill dishes from the cooler in small amounts instead of topping up an old, cooling tray.
Keep coleslaw and salad over ice or in the cooler, bringing out small amounts at a time.
Check hot food temperature once every hour during service and write it on the log.
At the end, do not mix leftovers back into fresh food, and do not take buffet leftovers home for resale.

blocks.text: After the event, bring dirty pots back separately from clean items, wash and dry everything the same day, and note what you forgot or ran short of. Next time the checklist is better.

takeaways: Build the timetable backwards from serving time with buffers
Separate raw, cooking and ready-to-eat zones
Preheat coolers, fill them well and keep cold food in a separate cooler
Use a written equipment checklist for every job

activity.title: Plan your production day
steps: Pick your 100-guest menu from the last lesson.
Write a timetable working back from a 1:00 pm serving, including travel and set-up.
Draw a simple sketch of your kitchen showing raw, cooking and ready-to-eat zones.
Write your equipment checklist under the five groups.
Mark the buffers in your timetable in a different colour.
activity.evidence: Your timetable, kitchen zone sketch and equipment checklist

quiz.q: Ngozi uses 120 g of raw rice per guest and a 10% buffer. How much raw rice should she plan for 100 guests?
quiz.explain: 100 × 120 g = 12 kg, and 12 × 1.1 = 13.2 kg. She would round up to buy about 14 kg.

quiz.q: A recipe serves 10 and uses 300 g onions. How many onions for 50 servings?
quiz.explain: The scaling factor is 50 ÷ 10 = 5, and 300 g × 5 = 1.5 kg.

quiz.q: Which dish is the riskiest to include in a food-pack order held for 3 hours?
options: Fried plantain added early and held hot
quiz.explain: Fried plantain softens badly when held. It is better fried at the venue or left off the menu for long holds.

quiz.q: Serving is at 2:00 pm and the venue is 1 hour away. Set-up takes 45 minutes and she wants a 30-minute buffer. When should she leave?
quiz.explain: Working back: 2:00 pm minus 45 minutes set-up is 1:15 pm, minus a 30-minute buffer means arriving by 12:45 pm, and minus 1 hour of travel means leaving at 11:45 am.

quiz.q: Why should she preheat an insulated cooler before packing hot rice?
options: So the cold walls do not cool the food into the danger zone
quiz.explain: A cold cooler draws heat out of the food. Preheating with hot water helps the rice stay above 60°C longer.

quiz.q: Which kitchen layout best prevents cross-contamination?
options: One table for everything to save space
Raw meat cut next to the coleslaw so tasks finish faster
Separate raw, cooking and ready-to-eat zones with handwashing between them
Washing the board only at the end of the day
quiz.explain: Zoning keeps raw juices away from food that will not be cooked again, and handwashing stops germs moving on hands.

modules.title: Costing, Allergens and Running a Professional Service
modules.overview: Good food at a loss is not a business. This module shows you how to cost every plate and set a price with real profit, how to manage allergens and special diets honestly, and how to write quotations, take deposits safely and keep records that make each job better than the last.

lessons.title: Costing per plate and setting a profitable price
objectives: List every cost in a catering job, including hidden ones
Calculate the cost per plate from a full job budget
Set a selling price using a chosen profit margin
Explain the difference between markup and margin

blocks.text: Many home cooks price by feel, or copy what someone else charges. Then they finish a big job tired, with almost nothing left. The cure is a costing sheet: every naira you will spend, divided by the number of plates, plus the profit you choose.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.caption: Keep every market receipt or note every price, because costing starts with real numbers.

blocks.text: The full list of costs

items: **Ingredients**: rice, meat, fish, tomatoes, pepper, onions, oil, seasoning, vegetables, drinks.
**Fuel**: cooking gas or charcoal, and generator fuel if power fails.
**Packaging**: food packs, spoons, serviettes, nylon bags, foil, labels.
**Labour**: helpers, servers, and a fair wage for your own time.
**Transport**: fuel, a hired car or dispatch rider, and venue loading.
**Equipment hire or wear**: chafing dishes, extra pots, coolers, and replacing broken items.
**Small extras**: ice, water for washing, cleaning materials, data and phone calls.

blocks.title: From costs to price per plate
items: Add all job costs
Divide by plates
Choose profit margin
Price = cost ÷ (1 − margin)
Round to clean price
blocks.caption: Use the same steps for every quote so your prices are consistent and defendable.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing 100 plates of jollof, chicken and coleslaw
blocks.context: For example, Ronke costs a 100-guest food-pack order in Lagos. All prices below are approximate examples only; use your own market prices on the day you quote.
steps: Rice 14 kg at about ₦1,800 per kg = ₦25,200. Chicken 14 birds at about ₦9,000 each = ₦126,000.
Tomatoes, pepper and onions about ₦30,000. Oil about ₦15,000. Seasoning and spices about ₦8,000. Coleslaw ingredients about ₦20,000. Ingredients total: ₦224,200.
Gas about ₦12,000. Packs, spoons and nylon for 110 packs about ₦22,000. Transport about ₦15,000. Two helpers at ₦10,000 each = ₦20,000.
blocks.result: Each plate costs Ronke about ₦2,932 before any profit. Anything she charges below that loses money.

blocks.text: Adding profit: margin versus markup

**Markup** is profit as a percentage of cost. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of the selling price. They are not the same, and mixing them up is a common reason caterers earn less than they think. If you want 30 percent of the money you receive to be profit, that is a 30 percent margin.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting Ronke's price
blocks.context: For example, Ronke decides she wants a 30% margin on this job, after paying herself through the labour line.
steps: She rounds to a clean figure: ₦4,200 per plate.
Profit: ₦420,000 − ₦293,200 = ₦126,800, which is about 30% of the price.
She notes the date of her market prices on the quote, because prices can change quickly.
blocks.result: Ronke quotes ₦4,200 per head (approximate example) and knows exactly where every naira goes.

blocks.title: Quote with a validity date
blocks.text: Food prices in Nigerian markets can rise between your quote and the event. Write 'This quote is valid for 7 days' or a similar period, and confirm prices again if the client books late.
Check your price against the market

Once you know your cost price, compare with what other caterers in your area charge for similar food. If your price is far higher, look for savings: buying rice and oil in bulk, sharing transport, or a smaller protein portion offered openly. If it is far lower, you may be underpricing your work. Never cut cost by cutting food safety: the thermometer, soap and ice packs stay.
Pay yourself on purpose

Your own hours of shopping, cooking, packing and delivering are a real cost. If you leave them out, your 'profit' is really your wage, and you cannot grow or hire help later. Put a labour line for yourself in every costing, at a daily rate you consider fair, separate from the profit margin. Profit is then what the business keeps for new pots, coolers, savings and bad months.

For big jobs, protein is usually the largest single cost, as in Ronke's example where chicken is over 40 percent of the total. Small changes there move your whole price: a smaller piece, a mix of chicken and beef, or buying whole birds and cutting them yourself instead of buying parts. Always tell the client what portion they are paying for so there are no surprises.

Keep your costing sheet as a simple table in a notebook, Excel or Google Sheets. After each job, compare planned costs with what you actually spent. Over time your estimates get sharper and your quotes faster.

takeaways: Count every cost: ingredients, fuel, packs, labour, transport, extras
Cost per plate = total job cost ÷ number of plates
Price with margin = cost ÷ (1 − margin)
A 30% markup is not a 30% margin
Date your prices and give quotes a validity period

activity.title: Cost one menu package
steps: Take your 100-guest quantity sheet from Module 2.
Visit or call your market and write current prices for each item.
Add fuel, packaging, labour, transport and extras.
Calculate cost per plate and a price at your chosen margin.
Compare your price with two other caterers in your area.
activity.evidence: A completed costing sheet with cost per plate, chosen margin and final price

lessons.title: Allergens, special diets and honest risk control
objectives: Name the common food allergens and where they hide in Nigerian dishes
Collect and record allergy information from clients
Prevent allergen cross-contact in preparation and serving
Respond correctly when a guest asks about ingredients

blocks.text: A food allergy is when the body's immune system reacts to a normal food as if it were dangerous. Reactions can be mild, like an itchy mouth, or severe and life-threatening, with swelling of the throat and difficulty breathing. Cooking does not remove most allergens. For an allergic guest, even a small trace from a shared spoon can be enough.

blocks.name: peanuts
blocks.caption: Groundnut hides in suya spice, sauces and snacks, so ask and label.

blocks.text: The common allergens

The UK Food Standards Agency lists 14 allergens that food businesses there must declare: celery, cereals containing gluten (such as wheat), crustaceans (such as crayfish, prawns and crab), eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs (such as snails and periwinkle), mustard, tree nuts, peanuts (groundnuts), sesame, soya, and sulphur dioxide or sulphites. Nigeria's rules may differ, but this list is a useful, recognised checklist for any caterer.

head: Allergen
Where it often hides in Nigerian party food
rows: Suya spice (yaji), groundnut soup, kuli-kuli, some pepper mixes and small chops
Ground crayfish in jollof, stews, egusi and other soups; prawns in fried rice
Snails and periwinkle in soups and peppered snacks
Boiled egg in moi moi or jollof, puff puff and cake batter, salad cream
Meat pie, chin chin, puff puff, spring roll and samosa wrappers, bread
Cake, chin chin, some sauces and drinks
Dried fish in soups, fish pie, stock
Some snacks, sauces and stock cubes: check labels

blocks.title: Allergen handling: risky versus safe
items: Risky habits
Safe habits
right: Allergies written on the job sheet
blocks.caption: Most allergen accidents come from habits, not from bad intentions.

blocks.text: Before the event: collect and record

items: Ask every client: 'Does any guest have a food allergy, or need halal, vegetarian or no-pork food?'
Write the answer on the job sheet, not only in a chat.
Keep a short ingredient list for every dish you make, including stock cubes and spice mixes.
Plan how the allergen-free portion will be cooked, packed and labelled.
Confirm the plan with the client in writing.

blocks.text: On the day: prevent cross-contact

**Cross-contact** is when a small amount of an allergen gets into a food that should not contain it. Cook the allergen-free portion first, in clean pots with clean spoons, before the kitchen is full of crayfish and groundnut dust. Pack it separately, seal it and label it clearly with the guest's name or the words 'No groundnut' or 'No crayfish'. Give it directly to the client or host, not to a general usher.

blocks.title: Worked example: one guest with a groundnut allergy
blocks.context: For example, Halima is catering 80 packs and the client says the bride's sister has a severe groundnut allergy. The menu includes suya-spiced chicken.
steps: She checks every dish: the suya spice contains groundnut, and her chin chin is fried in the same oil as groundnut snacks.
She cooks one pack first: plain peppered chicken, jollof rice and coleslaw, with clean pots, spoons and fresh oil.
She seals it in a separate container, labels it 'NO GROUNDNUT: for Aisha', and stores it in its own bag.
At the venue, she hands it to the client personally and explains what is in it.
She leaves chin chin out of that pack because she cannot guarantee no cross-contact.
blocks.result: The allergic guest gets a safe meal, the client sees real care, and Halima is honest about what she cannot guarantee.

blocks.title: If you do not know, say so
blocks.text: If a guest asks whether a dish contains an allergen and you are not sure, say 'I am not sure, so please do not eat it.' Never guess. If someone has trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or collapses after eating, call for emergency help and get them to a hospital immediately.
Other risks to control
Labelling dishes at a buffet

At a buffet, guests cannot ask you about every dish. Place a small card in front of each dish with its name and the main allergens it contains, for example 'Jollof rice: contains crayfish' or 'Chin chin: contains wheat, egg and milk'. Mark vegetarian and no-pork dishes clearly. Give each dish its own serving spoon, and tell servers not to move spoons between dishes, because a spoon from the groundnut sauce dipped into the plain rice puts the allergen on every plate that follows.

items: Food handlers with diarrhoea or vomiting should stay away from food work. The UK Food Standards Agency advises staying off until 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Cover cuts on hands with a waterproof plaster and wear a glove over it.
Respect religious diets honestly: never serve pork or non-halal meat as halal.
Apply the same safety standard to small jobs as to big ones.

takeaways: Allergens are not destroyed by cooking, and traces can harm
Crayfish, groundnut, egg and wheat hide in many Nigerian dishes
Record allergies on the job sheet and confirm the plan in writing
Cook, pack and label allergen-free meals first and separately
If unsure, tell the guest not to eat it

activity.title: Write ingredient cards
steps: List every dish in your menu package.
For each dish, write all ingredients, including stock cubes and spice mixes.
Mark any of the 14 allergens each dish contains.
Write how you would prepare an allergen-free version of your main plate.
Add an allergy question to your client enquiry form.
activity.evidence: Ingredient cards with allergens marked, and your updated enquiry form

lessons.title: Quotations, deposits, records and client feedback
objectives: Write a clear catering quotation with terms
Set and collect a deposit safely, avoiding payment scams
Keep a simple event record for every job
Use client feedback and numbers to improve the next job

blocks.text: Clients judge you before they taste your food. A clear quotation, a sensible deposit and on-time delivery tell them you are reliable. Simple records then turn each job into lessons, so your planning gets more accurate and your profit more predictable.

blocks.name: printing-invoices
blocks.caption: A written quote protects both you and your client.

blocks.text: What a quotation should contain

items: Your business name, phone number and, if you have one, your CAC registration name.
Client name, event date, venue, serving time and guest count.
Menu with portion sizes, for example one piece of chicken per pack.
Price per head and total, and what is included: packs, spoons, servers, transport, chafing dishes.
What is not included, for example drinks, venue kitchen fees, extra servers.
Deposit amount, balance due date and accepted payment methods.
Validity of the quote, and your cancellation and guest-count change terms.

blocks.title: Worked example: deposit and payment terms
blocks.context: For example, Ronke's quote for 100 food packs is ₦420,000 (approximate example). Her policy is a 50% deposit to confirm the booking and the balance two days before the event.
steps: Deposit: ₦420,000 × 0.50 = ₦210,000, paid before she buys any ingredient.
Balance: ₦420,000 − ₦210,000 = ₦210,000, due two days before the event.
Guest count changes: final number confirmed 5 days before; extra packs added at ₦4,200 each if she can cook them.
Cancellation: her written terms say the deposit covers ingredients already bought.
She sends a receipt for each payment on WhatsApp with the amount, date and balance remaining.
blocks.result: The client knows exactly what to pay and when, and Ronke never funds a party with her own money.

blocks.title: Avoid fake payment alerts
blocks.text: Fraudsters send fake SMS or screenshot alerts. Always confirm money has arrived by checking your banking app or account balance, not the SMS or screenshot. Payment links from Paystack, or transfers to your Moniepoint or OPay business account, give you a clear record.
Keep an event record
For each job, keep one page or one spreadsheet row. It takes 15 minutes after the event and is worth more than any memory.

head: Record
Example entry
rows: 14 kg rice, 6 packs of rice left over

blocks.title: The improvement cycle
items: Deliver the job
Record the numbers
Ask for feedback
Adjust plans and prices
blocks.caption: Each job's records make the next quote, shopping list and timetable more accurate.

blocks.text: Ask for feedback the right way

Within two days, send the client a short message: 'Thank you for choosing us. On a scale of 1 to 5, how was the food, the timing and our service? What one thing should we improve?' Ask permission to share a positive comment as a testimonial. Short, specific questions get real answers.
Numbers worth tracking

items: **Leftover rate**: packs left ÷ packs made. Six left from 110 is about 5%, close to your buffer.
**Cost accuracy**: actual cost ÷ planned cost. ₦301,500 ÷ ₦293,200 is about 1.03, or 3% over.
**On-time rate**: jobs served on time ÷ total jobs.
**Repeat and referral clients**: how many new jobs came from past clients.

blocks.text: Guest-count changes and cancellations

Guest numbers often change at Nigerian events. Protect yourself by agreeing a date for the final number, for example five days before the event, after which you charge for the number confirmed even if fewer guests come. If the client adds guests late, accept only what you can cook safely, at the per-head price. For cancellations, write that the deposit covers ingredients already bought and work already done. Put these terms on the quote so they are agreed before any money moves, not argued about afterwards.

items: A good receipt shows your business name, the client's name and event date.
It shows the amount paid, the payment method and the date received.
It shows the total job price and the balance still due.
Send it the same day as a WhatsApp image or PDF, and keep a copy in your job folder.

blocks.text: Register a business name with the CAC when you are ready, and use it on your quotes, receipts and account. Clients, especially offices and churches, are more comfortable paying into an account in a business name, and it keeps your records clean.

If the same problem appears in three jobs, such as always running short of chicken or food arriving lukewarm, fix the cause: change the portion plan, buy another cooler, or leave earlier. One bad day can be bad luck; a pattern is a planning problem.

takeaways: A quotation lists the menu, price, inclusions, deposit and terms
Collect a deposit before buying ingredients
Confirm payments in your banking app, never by SMS alone
Keep one event record per job and track leftovers, costs and timing
Use feedback patterns, not single events, to change your plans

activity.title: Create your quote and record templates
steps: Write a one-page quotation template with all the sections in this lesson.
Set your deposit, balance and cancellation terms.
Create an event record page or spreadsheet with the six columns shown.
Write your feedback message for clients.
Fill the templates in for your 100-guest practice event.
activity.evidence: Your quotation template, event record template and feedback message

quiz.q: A job costs ₦150,000 for 50 plates. What is the cost per plate?
Cost per plate is ₦3,000 and she wants a 25% margin. What is the price?
quiz.explain: Price = cost ÷ (1 − margin) = ₦3,000 ÷ 0.75 = ₦4,000. A 25% markup would give ₦3,750, which is a lower margin.

quiz.q: A client sends a screenshot showing a ₦200,000 transfer for the deposit. What should the caterer do before shopping?
options: Check her banking app to confirm the money has arrived
Ask the client for a second screenshot
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS can be faked. Only the balance or transaction in her own banking app confirms payment.

quiz.q: A guest has a crustacean allergy. Which dish is most likely to contain it?
options: Jollof rice made with ground crayfish
quiz.explain: Crayfish is a crustacean and is used in many Nigerian rice dishes, stews and soups.

quiz.q: A guest asks if the stew contains groundnut and the caterer is not sure. What should she say?
options: 'I am not sure, so please do not eat it'
quiz.explain: Never guess about allergens. Small traces can cause severe reactions.

quiz.q: Over three jobs, she has 20%, 18% and 22% of packs left over with a 10% buffer. What is the best response?
options: Reduce her portion or buffer plan and re-test her packs
quiz.explain: A consistent pattern well above her buffer means her portion sizes or buffer are too generous. She should adjust and re-test.

modules.title: Your Event Plan, Your Offer and Your Next Steps
modules.overview: You now bring everything together into one complete event plan with a food safety plan for each dish, learn to present your catering service clearly and honestly to clients, and set a 90-day plan for your first or next paid jobs.

lessons.title: Building your complete event plan and food safety plan
objectives: Assemble menu, quantities, costing and timetable into one event plan
Identify the main hazard and control at each step for each dish
Write a simple food safety plan with checks and records
Document a real or realistic event as capstone evidence

blocks.text: Your capstone is one complete plan for a real or realistic event. It should be good enough that another trained cook could follow it and deliver the job safely. You already have most of the parts from earlier lessons. This lesson shows how to join them and add a written food safety plan.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking a large checklist
blocks.caption: A complete plan is a checklist you can follow on a busy day.

blocks.text: The six parts of your event plan

blocks.title: Capstone event plan contents
items: Client and event details
Menu with portion sizes
Quantity and shopping sheet
Costing and quotation
Production timetable
Food safety plan and logs
blocks.caption: Tick each part before you call the plan complete.

blocks.text: Thinking in hazards and controls

Professional food businesses use a system called **HACCP**, Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. You do not need the full system for small events, but its thinking is simple and powerful: for each step a food goes through, ask **what could go wrong** (the hazard), **what stops it** (the control), and **how will I check** (the record). The steps are usually buying, storing, preparing, cooking, cooling, reheating, holding, transporting and serving.

head: Step
Hazard
Control
Check and record
rows: Buy from a clean, cool seller; go straight home
Freeze or chill below 5°C, raw below cooked
Preheated coolers, filled hot, lids shut
Clean serving spoons, labelled allergen-free packs

blocks.title: Worked example: a food safety plan for coleslaw
blocks.context: For example, Funmi is writing the safety plan for 9 kg of coleslaw for a 100-guest event. Coleslaw is never cooked, so control matters at every step.
steps: Buying: she chooses firm, fresh cabbage and carrots, and buys salad cream with an intact seal and a valid date.
Preparing: she washes the vegetables in safe water, uses the green ready-to-eat board and washes her hands first.
Storing: the shredded vegetables go into covered containers in the fridge below 5°C overnight.
Mixing: she adds the dressing on the morning of the event in a sanitised bowl and keeps it chilled.
Transport and serving: it travels in a separate cooler with ice packs; she records 4°C at packing and checks again on arrival.
blocks.result: Each step has a named hazard, a control and a recorded check, which is exactly what the capstone asks for.

blocks.text: Logs that prove your practice

Your plan should include blank log sheets you will fill on the day: a temperature log (dish, time, reading, initials), a cleaning check (zones wiped and sanitised, time), and an allergy log (guest, allergen, how the pack was prepared and who received it). Photos also help: your zones set up, a thermometer reading, labelled allergen-free packs.

blocks.title: If you have not catered yet
blocks.text: Choose a realistic client, such as a friend's 50-guest birthday, and do a test cook of one dish at small scale. Time it, weigh portions, and take temperature readings. Real numbers from a small test make a planning exercise far more convincing.
After the event: the debrief

items: Fill your event record: costs, quantities, leftovers, timing, temperatures.
Collect client feedback with your short message.
Write three things that went well and three you will change.
Update your menu, quantity sheet or timetable templates.
File photos, logs and receipts together in one folder.

blocks.text: Organising your capstone folder

Keep one folder, paper or on Google Drive, with a section for each part of the plan. Name files clearly, for example '01 Client details', '02 Menu and portions', '03 Quantities', '04 Costing and quote', '05 Timetable', '06 Safety plan and logs', '07 Debrief'. A reviewer, or a future client asking how you work, should be able to open it and understand your job in a few minutes.

items: Photo of your kitchen zones set up before cooking.
Photo of a probe thermometer reading in a pot of rice or a chicken piece.
Photo of packed coolers and the separate cold cooler.
Photo of a labelled allergen-free pack, if you prepared one.
Photo of the finished pack or buffet table as the client saw it.

blocks.text: Write your plan in plain words a helper can follow. 'Check chicken at 70°C' is clearer than 'cook properly'. 'Leave at 11:00 am' is clearer than 'leave early'. Clear instructions are part of food safety, because a confused helper is the one most likely to skip a step.

Whether your event is real or a detailed plan, honesty is what makes it valuable. If something went wrong, such as rice reading 55°C on arrival, write it down with what you will change. A plan that shows problems and fixes shows more skill than one that claims everything was perfect.

takeaways: Your capstone joins menu, quantities, costing, timetable and safety plan
For each step ask: hazard, control, check
Logs and photos are evidence of safe practice
A debrief after every job keeps your templates improving

activity.title: Draft your food safety plan
steps: Choose the two highest-risk dishes on your capstone menu.
For each, fill a hazard, control, check table for every step from buying to serving.
Prepare a blank temperature log and allergy log.
Do a small test cook of one dish and record real temperatures.
Add the tables and logs to your capstone folder.
activity.evidence: Hazard and control tables for two dishes and a filled test-cook temperature log

lessons.title: Presenting your catering service to clients
objectives: Describe your service in specific, trustworthy terms
Build a simple menu and price list for WhatsApp
Use photos, tastings and testimonials honestly
Discuss capacity and terms confidently with a client

blocks.text: Clients hear 'my food is delicious' from every caterer. What wins bookings is specific proof that you are delicious **and** reliable: clear packages, honest photos, real reviews, and simple facts about how you keep food safe and arrive on time.

blocks.name: order-food
blocks.alt: A person ordering food on a phone
blocks.caption: Most Nigerian catering enquiries start on WhatsApp, so make your offer easy to read there.

blocks.title: Vague pitch versus specific pitch
items: Vague
Specific
blocks.caption: Specific details build trust because a client can check them.

blocks.text: Your one-page offer

items: Business name, area you cover, and contact number.
Two or three packages with dishes, portion sizes and price per head (marked as current and subject to market changes).
What is included: packs, cutlery, transport, servers, chafing dishes.
Your booking terms: deposit, balance date, minimum order, notice needed.
Two or three lines on food safety: thermometer checks, hot holding, allergen-free packs on request.
Two or three real client testimonials, with permission.

blocks.title: Worked example: replying to a WhatsApp enquiry
blocks.context: For example, a client messages Ngozi: 'Hi, how much for food for my mum's 60th, about 70 people, next month?'
steps: Ngozi replies within the hour, thanks her and asks for the date, venue, serving time, format (packs or buffet) and any allergies.
She sends her package sheet: Package A jollof, chicken, moi moi, coleslaw at about ₦4,200 per head; Package B fried rice, turkey, plantain, salad at about ₦5,500 per head (approximate examples).
She calculates 70 × ₦4,200 = ₦294,000 for Package A and 70 × ₦5,500 = ₦385,000 for Package B.
She explains: 'Food is held above 60°C in insulated coolers and we arrive at least one hour before serving.'
She offers a paid tasting of two dishes and states the 50% deposit to confirm the date.
blocks.result: The client receives a fast, clear and specific answer with two priced choices, instead of a single vague figure.

blocks.text: Photos and tastings

Use photos of your own food, taken in daylight on a clean surface, showing a real pack or plate as the client will receive it. Never use internet photos of other caterers' food: clients notice, and it destroys trust. A WhatsApp Business account lets you add a catalogue with photos and package prices, and set quick replies for common questions. Tastings work well for weddings and big events; many caterers charge a small fee and subtract it from the final bill if the client books.

blocks.title: Testimonials need permission
blocks.text: Before sharing a client's message or photo of their event, ask. Remove phone numbers and private details. A first name and event type, such as 'Bisi, 50th birthday', is enough.
Talking about capacity honestly

When a job is too big or too soon, say so and offer an alternative: a smaller menu, a later date, or partnering with another trusted caterer with clear roles. Clients remember the caterer who was honest more than the one who overpromised and arrived late. Equally, when you can do the job, state your plan confidently: how many helpers, when you will arrive, and how food will be kept hot.
Fast, polite replies win jobs

Many clients message three or four caterers and book the first one who answers clearly. Set up WhatsApp Business quick replies for the questions you get most: your packages and prices, the information you need for a quote, your deposit terms, and the areas you cover. Reply within a few hours where you can, even if only to say you will send a full quote by evening. Always confirm bookings in writing with the date, menu, number, price and deposit received.

items: Quick reply 1: 'Thank you for contacting us. Please send the date, venue, serving time, number of guests and any allergies.'
Quick reply 2: your package sheet image with current prices and validity date.
Quick reply 3: your deposit, balance and cancellation terms.
Quick reply 4: a booking confirmation template with all agreed details.

blocks.text: After each event, post two or three of your own photos on WhatsApp Status with a short caption, such as '120 packs for a 50th birthday in Ikeja, served hot at 1 pm'. Do not show guests' faces without permission. Regular, real posts remind your contacts that you cater and show the size of jobs you can handle.

Finally, keep your promises small and exact. If you say you will arrive at 11:45 am, arrive at 11:45 am. If a pack contains one piece of chicken, never quietly reduce it. Every job you deliver exactly as described becomes the strongest advertising you have.

head: Client says
Strong reply
rows: Offer a smaller protein or one fewer side, not lower safety
State your real capacity, then suggest a partner or a smaller scope
Explain that the balance is due before the event, as in your terms

takeaways: Specific, checkable details win more bookings than general praise
Keep a one-page offer with packages, prices and terms
Use only your own food photos, and testimonials with permission
Be honest about capacity and firm about payment terms

steps: Write two or three packages with portions and current prices.
Add inclusions, booking terms and three food safety lines.
Photograph one of your dishes in a real pack in daylight.
Ask one past client or tester for a short testimonial.
Save it as an image or PDF to send on WhatsApp.

lessons.title: Certification, registration options and your 90-day plan
objectives: Check your capstone evidence against the certificate requirements
Identify registration and compliance steps to ask about as you grow
Set realistic 90-day goals for paid catering jobs
Choose skills to keep building after the course

blocks.text: This last lesson prepares you for the final quiz and certificate, and helps you plan the next three months. Your certificate means you can plan and deliver a catering job safely. Your evidence folder is what proves it.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate is backed by a real plan, real numbers and real safety records.

blocks.text: Check your evidence

items: A complete menu with portion sizes and calculated quantities for a stated guest count.
A costing sheet showing cost per plate and your price.
A production timetable working back from serving time.
A food safety plan with hazard, control and check for each high-risk dish.
Temperature and allergy logs, and photos, from a real event or a test cook.
A short reflection: what worked, what you will change.

blocks.text: Registration and compliance as you grow

Rules can differ by state and change over time, so check with the right offices rather than relying on hearsay. The **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)** registers business names, which helps you open a business bank account and look professional on quotes. If you later package food to sell in shops, such as bottled zobo, chin chin or spice mixes, products generally need **NAFDAC** registration; NAFDAC has guidance for micro and small businesses on its website. Some venues, offices and state authorities may ask food handlers for health checks or permits, so ask your local government environmental health office what applies where you work.

blocks.title: Your 90-day catering plan
items: Days 1 to 30: test and price
Days 31 to 60: first paid jobs
Days 61 to 90: review and grow
blocks.caption: Grow in steps: test, deliver, then review your records before taking bigger jobs.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Amaka finishes the course with a capstone plan for a 50-guest birthday and no paid jobs yet.
steps: Days 1 to 30: she does two test cooks for family events, records temperatures and portions, buys a probe thermometer and a second cooler, and finalises her one-page offer.
Days 31 to 60: she shares the offer on WhatsApp Status and with her church group, and aims for two paid jobs of 30 to 50 guests, each with a 50% deposit.
Days 61 to 90: she reviews her event records: leftovers, cost accuracy and timing. She adjusts portions and prices, collects two testimonials and decides whether to accept jobs up to 80 guests.
Throughout: she keeps every receipt and log in one folder per job.
blocks.result: Amaka grows from home cook to paid caterer in measured steps, with evidence at each step showing she is ready for the next size.

blocks.text: Skills to keep building

items: Food safety: take a recognised food hygiene course when you can, and keep reading WHO food safety material.
Menu range: master one new dish that holds well, such as fried rice or ofada sauce.
Business: bookkeeping in a simple spreadsheet, and separating business and personal money.
Team: train helpers on handwashing, zones and temperature checks before each job.

blocks.title: Keep your templates alive
blocks.text: Your enquiry form, quantity sheet, costing sheet, timetable, checklists and logs are your business system. Update them after every job and they will save you hours and protect your guests.
Measuring your first 90 days

At day 90, look at your event records and answer a few honest questions. How many paid jobs did you deliver, and how many enquiries became bookings? Was every job served on time? Did your actual costs stay close to your planned costs? Were leftovers close to your buffer, or far above it? Did any client book again or refer a friend? These numbers tell you whether to grow the size of jobs, raise prices, buy more equipment or first fix a weak spot.

Keep business money separate from household money from the start. Open a separate account or wallet for catering, put every deposit and balance into it, and pay ingredients, gas and helpers from it. At the end of each month, write the total received, total spent and what is left. This simple habit shows whether catering is really earning, and it makes registration, loans or grants easier later because you can show real records.

Before you sit the final quiz, revisit the numbers that matter most: 70°C at the centre when cooking, above 60°C for hot holding, below 5°C for cold holding, no more than 2 hours at room temperature, portion × guests + buffer, and price = cost ÷ (1 − margin). If you can explain each one with an example from your own plan, you are ready.

You started this course as a good cook. You finish it able to plan quantities with arithmetic, cost every plate, keep food out of the danger zone, protect allergic guests, and present a professional offer. Those habits are what let clients trust you with their most important days.

takeaways: Your evidence folder proves your skill: plans, numbers, logs and photos
CAC registers business names; packaged food products generally need NAFDAC registration
Ask your local environmental health office what applies in your state
Grow in steps: test, deliver small jobs, review, then grow

activity.title: Write your 90-day plan
steps: Check your capstone folder against the evidence list and fill any gaps.
Write one goal for each 30-day block, with a number of jobs or guests.
List the equipment you will buy first and its approximate cost.
Name one office you will contact to ask about registration or permits.
Share your plan with a friend or mentor who will check on you.
